messages.subject: Estimates with linearComb
parts:

Imagine a model (p~covariate1, psi~covariate1) using the occu

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] Estimates with linearComb
parts:
Dear Aude,

you can get estimates from the model by hand or use the functionality of unmarked.

(a) You can type plogis(X) for a logit-scale parameter or prediction X (for occupancy or detection) to backtransform it from the logit to the probability scale. This will however not give you a SE or confidence interval
(b) For a "Null model", with just an intercept in the state and the detection model (i.e., for the model you imagine), you can use backTransform(), which will also yield a SE.
(c) For models with covariates, use predict, which will also yield SEs and 95% CIs.

Check the vignettes that come with unmarked. There is information on this in "Overview of unmarked" and also "Dynamic occupancy models in unmarked". Both are relevant for your occupancy model.

Regards -- Marc

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: AW: [unmarked] Re: Estimates with linearComb
parts:
Dear Aude,

if you want to characterise the average occupancy probability and the average detection probability, then this approach is fine, what concerns the mean. However, for the standard error you would have to use the delta rule: you can't simply average the standard errors !

An alternative would be to fit the mean-centered covariates, in which case the intercept would represent the logit-scale occupancy and detection values for a typical covariate value, namely the mean of the observed values. You could then directly backtransform that to get both the estimate at the probability scale and its uncertainty (SE).

Centering covariates is very useful for interpretation of regression relationships, because it makes the intercept directly interpretable, something it is usually not, when it means the value of the response at a value of x=0.

Regards --- Marc

backtransform with the intercept to obtain my estimate.

Thank you very much for your advices. It helps me a lot.

Regards,

Aude

On 12 juin, 10:56, Kery Marc <marc.k...@vogelwarte.ch> wrote:
> Dear Aude,
>
> if you want to characterise the average occupancy probability and the average detection probability, then this approach is fine, what concerns the mean. However, for the standard error you would have to use the delta rule: you can't simply average the standard errors !
>
> An alternative would be to fit the mean-centered covariates, in which case the intercept would represent the logit-scale occupancy and detection values for a typical covariate value, namely the mean of the observed values. You could then directly backtransform that to get both the estimate at the probability scale and its uncertainty (SE).
>
> Centering covariates is very useful for interpretation of regression relationships, because it makes the intercept directly interpretable, something it is usually not, when it means the value of the response at a value of x=0.
>
> Regards  ---  Marc
